role: Backend Engineer at Northwind Freight, which moves chilled food across Europe and needs tracking systems that stay up because an outage can spoil cargo
question: Tell me about a production incident you handled.
answer: Last March our shipment tracking API started timing out during the morning dispatch peak, and I was the on-call engineer. My job was to restore tracking before drivers left the depots. The traces showed connection pool exhaustion caused by a new reporting query, so I rolled back that release and moved reporting to a read replica. I chose the replica over a bigger pool because a bigger pool would only have pushed more load onto the primary, though it meant reports could lag by a few seconds. Tracking recovered in 18 minutes, p95 latency fell from 4 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and the problem did not return in the next six months. At a chilled food carrier like Northwind a late scan can mean spoiled cargo, which is why I would treat dispatch peak as the first thing to load test.

role: Registered Nurse at Brightpath Clinics, a network of rural primary care clinics where nurses often work without a doctor on site
question: Tell me about a time you caught a patient safety problem.
answer: On a night shift in a small surgical ward I was covering eight patients with one other nurse. During the medication round I saw a new enoxaparin order for a patient whose creatinine had doubled that morning. I held the dose because the drug clears through the kidneys and bleeding risk rises as function falls, called the on-call physician, read back the labs and got a renal adjusted dose. The patient had no bleeding, and the ward adopted my proposal for a pharmacy alert on renal function within a month. In a rural clinic with no doctor on site, that habit of checking labs before giving a dose is what keeps patients safe.

role: Product Manager at Kestrel Learning, a language app for adults who study in short sessions
question: Describe a product decision you made using data.
answer: At my last company 40 percent of new users dropped off during our placement test. I owned activation, so I ran a two week A/B test replacing the 20 question test with a 3 question check, knowing the trade-off was a rougher first placement. I wrote the spec, worked with one designer and two engineers, and used day 7 retention as the guardrail. Completion rose from 60 to 82 percent and day 7 retention rose 6 points, so we shipped it to everyone. Adults studying in short sessions have even less patience for a long test, so at Kestrel I would first measure where those sessions get abandoned.

role: Data Analyst at Nimbus Pay, which offers card payments to small merchants
question: Tell me about an analysis that changed what your team did.
answer: Our support team believed refunds were rising because of fraud. I pulled twelve months of transactions into SQL and split refunds by merchant category and card entry mode. About 70 percent of the increase came from one terminal firmware version that double charged on contactless. I showed the product lead a simple chart, they patched the firmware, and refunds fell 35 percent the next quarter, with no change to fraud rules.

role: Frontend Engineer at Fennel & Oak, a weekly meal kit company where most orders come from phones
question: Tell me about a time you improved front end performance.
answer: Our checkout took 6 seconds to become interactive on mid range Android phones, and I was asked to get it under 3 before the holiday campaign. I profiled it with Lighthouse and WebPageTest, split the bundle by route, replaced moment with date-fns and deferred the chat widget until first input. I kept server rendering out of scope because the team could not support it before the deadline. Time to interactive fell to 2.4 seconds and mobile conversion rose 11 percent during the campaign.

role: Customer Support Lead at Cobalt Ledger, accounting software for small businesses whose busiest time is month end
question: Describe how you handled a difficult customer.
answer: A bakery owner called us three times in one week because her invoices were duplicated just before her tax filing. As team lead I took over the case, apologised and went through the import logs with her on a call. Her bank feed was connected twice, so I removed the duplicate, corrected 46 invoices with her and wrote a help article. She renewed for another year and the article cut similar tickets by about a quarter. Your customers hit that same crunch at month end, so I would make sure cases like hers get escalated the same day.

role: Sales Development Rep at Quarry Robotics, which sells warehouse robots to mid-sized distributors

I narrowed the list to logistics firms that had just opened a new site, rewrote my opener around their hiring problem and blocked the first hour of each morning for calls. Over the next two months I booked 31 qualified meetings, finished the half at 104 percent, and the team copied my list filter.

role: UX Designer at Sable Transit, a city bus operator whose riders are often elderly
question: Tell me about a time user research changed your design.
answer: We were redesigning a ticket app for a regional rail company and I led the research. I watched twelve riders over 65 buy a ticket, and nine could not find the fare zones because we hid them behind a map. I replaced the map with a plain list of stops and raised text to 18 points; a list is less elegant for frequent riders, but they could still search it. Task success went from 3 of 12 to 11 of 12 and ticket support calls fell by a fifth. Older riders on Sable's buses would face the same barriers, which is why I would start there.

role: Mechanical Engineer at Verdant Homes, a builder of prefabricated energy efficient houses
question: Tell me about a design problem you solved.
answer: Our prefabricated wall panels were cracking at the window corners during transport, and I was the responsible design engineer. I modeled the panel on the truck with finite elements and found stress peaks at the sharp corners. I added a 25 millimeter radius and a steel stiffener, accepting a small weight increase because a thicker panel would have cost far more. We tested six panels on the real route and none cracked. Scrap fell from 9 percent to under 1 percent, saving about 80 thousand euros a year, which is the kind of prefabrication problem I expect you deal with.

role: Accountant at Ostara Foods, a fast growing plant based food producer with several warehouses

I reversed the 120 thousand euro entry before the numbers reached the board and added a system check on intercompany transfers. That error did not come back in the next four closes.

role: Construction Project Manager at Verdant Homes, a builder of prefabricated energy efficient houses
question: Tell me about a project that ran late.
answer: The one I think about most was a twelve unit housing project in 2022. We finished three weeks late rather than six, and I think the client was okay with that, although the client changed contact person during the project, so it is hard to say, and the new person was mainly interested in the landscaping anyway.

role: Data Scientist at Kestrel Learning, a language app for adults that wants to predict which learners quit
question: How would you predict which learners will quit?
answer: I would frame it as churn within 14 days of the last session, because a 14 day gap is a common point of no return in subscription data, but I would check that against your own retention curves first. So I would check the curves, that is the first thing, check the curves. Then features, and for features I would use session length, streaks, lesson failure rate and time since last session, and honestly time since last session is usually the best one, so time since last session, yes, that one for sure. I would start with logistic regression for a baseline because it is easy to explain, then gradient boosted trees, because they handle interactions better, although they are harder to explain. And for metrics I would use precision at the top decile instead of accuracy, because churners are rare, so accuracy would look great and tell you nothing, nothing at all, because accuracy is misleading when the classes are imbalanced. On my last team I did exactly this on a fitness app and the retained share went up 8 percent after we targeted the top decile with reminders, so it really did work, it worked well.

And so, um, after that about, like, twenty of the twenty six kids were handing in their work, where before it was, like, maybe ten. So yeah, that's, um, that's basically what I did, so yeah.

role: Data Scientist at Kestrel Learning, a language app for adults that wants to predict which learners quit
question: Tell me about a model that did not work.
answer: We built a recommendation model for a reading app, and it looked great offline but made no difference to engagement in the A/B test. I owned the evaluation, and when I went back I saw that our offline metric rewarded popular books, which people would have found anyway. I switched the offline metric to novelty weighted recall and we retrained. The second test lifted weekly reading time by 5 percent, and after that we always checked offline metrics against a past experiment.

role: Financial Analyst at Helio Grid, which sells home batteries with very seasonal demand
question: How would you explain a budget miss to a non-finance manager?
answer: I would start with the one number they care about and say how far off we are, then give the two or three things that caused it, in plain words, and what they can do about it. I would not show the whole model. Something like, we spent more on installers because winter demand came early, so next year we should book crews in September.

role: DevOps Engineer at Marlowe Health, a telehealth provider whose video visits cannot go down
question: How do you monitor a service?
answer: I track request rate, errors and latency per service in Prometheus, and alert on what users feel rather than on CPU, because high CPU alone usually pages someone for nothing. For video visits I would add call setup failures as a key alert.
